Quick Read

Soros Fund Management bought Intel (INTC) up 28-fold to $340 million, its largest stock holding, before the shares dropped 50% from September 30.

Only put options on XLE and XOP outranked Intel in the fund's portfolio, while it cut NVIDIA (NVDA) shares 19%.

Weak fourth-quarter guidance and no expected free cash flow triggered Intel's 29% October 30 plunge, its worst day in over 50 years.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Soros Fund Management filed its third-quarter 13F at 4:05 p.m. ET on Friday, November 13, 2026. The filing names Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) as the fund's largest common-stock holding on September 30. A 13F is the quarterly list of U.S. stock holdings that large managers must file.

24/7 Wall St.

The fund owned 2,830,000 Intel shares, up from 100,000 at June 30, which made the stake roughly 28 times larger. It reported the position at $340,250,900, or 4.0% of a $8.51 billion portfolio spread across 263 positions.

Intel then fell by half. It closed at $59.66 on November 13, down 2.52% on the day and 50.4% below its September 30 close of $120.23. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), which the fund cut, fell 2.01% in the same session.

INTC Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What Soros' Fund Disclosed

The fund is run by CEO and chief investment officer Dawn Fitzpatrick. Its Intel value matches the September 30 closing price, so it shows the stake at quarter-end prices, which can differ from what the fund paid.

Only two lines were larger, and both were put options, which are contracts that gain value when prices fall. One was $670.2 million of puts on the Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLE), and the other was $327.5 million of puts on the SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETF (NYSEARCA:XOP).

title: Intel CEO’s warning offers a 2027 signal for Micron investors
detail:
Intel CEO’s warning offers a 2027 signal for Micron investors
Moz Farooque, Celine Provini
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 1:06 PM PST 4 min read
INTC
MU
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

I covered in a recent story how I was pricing out a storage upgrade for my PlayStation 5 because I needed more room for Grand Theft Auto 6.

Then I saw what the SSD I wanted would cost. Suddenly, I was far less worried about making room for the game than making room in my budget.

Perhaps the sticker shock reminded me of a story I wrote in October, when Intel warned that rising memory costs were slowing down PC demand. The AI boom continues to drive production toward high-bandwidth memory used in data centers, leaving far less capacity for conventional RAM. 

My PS5 drive uses flash storage, not RAM, but both continue to get more expensive as demand for AI hardware grows.

Intel (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan told Yahoo Finance that buyers willing to pay more might not get enough memory. For Micron (MU) investors, it's a strong signal that its pricing power could last well into 2027.

Intel's memory warning goes beyond sticker shock

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan believes that even with buyers willing to pay higher prices for memory, they might not be able to get it.

"Yes, six, seven times. And even if you're willing to pay, you may not get it," he said, arguing that the shortage could get a lot worse in 2027. 

TrendForce offers a clearer yardstick. 

In September, it forecast that conventional DRAM contract prices would rise 10% to 15% from the prior quarter in the final three months of 2026, with NAND flash up 15% to 20%, with the pressure extending far beyond the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators.

That plays right into Micron's proverbial hands, and its recent results show what a tight market can mean on the selling side.

Fiscal Q4 sales climbed to $54.23 billion from $11.32 billion a year earlier. Adjusted earnings rose to $33.42 a share from $3.03, and adjusted gross margin reached 87%.

The question for investors isn't whether the squeeze has helped Micron. It's how much longer it can.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warns the memory shortage could worsen in 2027.Bloomberg / Getty Images
Micron has already locked in higher prices for much of 2027

Tan described Intel's comeback as "a multi-year turnaround." 

The memory shortage in many ways explains why even a better processor might not be able to fix everything. A PC maker needs enough affordable RAM to build a machine customers will buy. 

Micron is on the other side of that negotiation, and some of its customers are committing well before they need the chips.

Key Takeaways

AMD fell 9% today, giving back part of this week's roughly 30% gain after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned.

That gain came from Nvidia's turmoil, and fast money leaves fast.

Marvell, Intel and Arm fell with AMD as the 10-year yield climbed above 5%.

Analysts expect AMD's normalized EPS to more than double in 2027, and Nvidia's report next Tuesday is the next test.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) fell 9% today, giving back part of the roughly 30% it gained this week after Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) CEO Jensen Huang resigned.

AMD put out no news of its own, and investors sold the whole chip group, Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ), Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) and Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) included.

Easy come, easy go

Huang resigned on Thursday, and investors piled into AMD as the obvious alternative. Today some of that money went back out.

Nvidia fell 2% after HSBC cut it to Hold. The 10-year yield also hit 5.17% after a hot wholesale inflation reading, and higher yields hurt stocks priced on profits years out.

Nobody got a pass

Marvell fell 5% with no news of its own. It agreed to buy Lumentum on Nov. 2 and said its fiscal third-quarter revenue was in line with guidance, so its Dec. 1 report is its chance to show the selling was about the group.

The server CPU makers fell together, too: Intel slipped 3% and Arm 5%. UBS's Timothy Arcuri estimates third-quarter server CPU shipments rose 31% from a year earlier, with Arm's unit share up to 20.1%, Intel's down to 51.5% and AMD's roughly flat at 28.4%. When all three fall at once, investors are questioning how long that market keeps growing.

The numbers still hold up

Analysts expect AMD's normalized EPS to more than double in 2027:

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That 2027 estimate was $15.76 on Oct. 23. Most of the jump comes from Helios, AMD's rack-scale GPU system, already running workloads for OpenAI, Meta and others.

AMD traded at 39x forward earnings at the last close. That's above its five-year average of about 35x but far below the 67x it hit in June:

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Today's drop takes it to about 35x, right around that average. The risk is the customers paying for those racks: OpenAI, which holds up to 6 gigawatts of Helios commitments, posted a $10.9 billion adjusted operating loss in its third quarter, The Wall Street Journal reported.

title: AMD or Intel: 1 Chip Stock Is the Clear Winner
detail:
AMD or Intel: 1 Chip Stock Is the Clear Winner
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 10:50 AM PST 5 min read
INTC
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC), two of the leading semiconductor companies, are capitalizing on the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Both stocks have performed well as a result. AMD's shares are up 158% this year, while Intel's have gained 69%, as of writing. Both companies could continue to ride the AI tailwind, provided infrastructure spending continues to grow. But which of these two chip stocks is the better buy right now?

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Comparing their financial results

AMD and Intel have both been posting excellent financial results. Let's start with the latter. Intel's third-quarter revenue increased by 21% year over year to $16.5 billion. Gross profit jumped 36% year over year with a 44.1% non-GAAP margin, versus the margin of 40% reported in the prior-year quarter. Intel's non-GAAP net earnings per share (EPS) were $0.52, up 126% year over year. Importantly, the company's data center and AI segment posted $7.3 billion in revenue, up 78% year over year.

This business is now the company's most important growth driver, and it should remain so over the medium term. In fact, Intel's Client Computing and Physical AI Group segment posted $8.1 billion in revenue, down 5% year over year. For the fourth quarter, Intel expects revenue of $15.5 billion at the midpoint, representing a 13% year-over-year increase. Its projected non-GAAP EPS of $0.25 would increase 67% from the year-ago period.

Now turning to AMD, the company's third-quarter revenue increased 45% year-over-year to $13.4 billion. Gross profit was up 51% to $7.2 billion, with a 54% gross margin, versus the 52% margin reported in the year-ago period. AMD's non-GAAP EPS jumped 74% year over year to $2.09. The company's data center segment did much of the heavy lifting, recording $8.5 billion in revenue, up 97% from the prior-year quarter.

And AMD's fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $17 billion at the midpoint would represent year-over-year revenue growth of 66%. So, by next quarter, AMD could generate higher revenue than Intel while also growing its revenue faster and boasting stronger gross margins. True, Intel's EPS is growing faster, but AMD's is higher, and the company also boasts stronger net profit margins.

And within their all-important data center businesses, AMD is growing much faster as well. So, overall, AMD's financial results look stronger right now. The company wins this category hands down.

Stocks opened higher Friday after mixed inflation data, but turned lower on continued weakness in tech stocks. Still, the three main benchmarks closed with impressive weekly gains. Looking ahead, there's plenty on next week's docket to keep markets volatile, including Nvidia's (NVDA) first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm and the highly anticipated Anthropic IPO.

At the close, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was down 0.9% at 25,136 and the broader S&P 500 was off 0.4% at 7,561. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 0.1% at 52,347.

Ahead of the open, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the Producer Price Index (PPI), which measures wholesale prices, rose 0.3% from September to October — lower than economists' 0.4% forecast. But PPI was up 6.5% year over year, the highest annual rate since November 2022.

Core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% month over month, in line with expectations. However, core PPI's annual rate of 5% was the highest since January 2023.

"The good news is that producer price inflation cooled from September," says Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors. "The bad news is that it may not have cooled enough to give markets the rate relief they want."

Indeed, rate-hike odds rose after this morning's PPI. According to CME Group FedWatch, futures traders are now pricing in a 90% probability the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting, up from 85% one day ago.

title: What Is Going On With Intel Stock After Its Earnings Call?
detail:
What Is Going On With Intel Stock After Its Earnings Call?
Trefis Team
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 8:53 AM PST 4 min read
INTC
^GSPC
AMD
NVDA
QCOM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

The past month has been painful for Intel (INTC) shareholders. The stock lost 37.6% from October 14 to November 12, compared with a 1.6% slip for the S&P 500. The sharpest drop occurred on October 30, when shares fell 28.6% the day after the company's fiscal Q3 2026 earnings call. On that call, management forecast lower fourth-quarter revenue, even though Intel's data center chips had just posted their fastest growth in 15 years. So which part of Intel is shrinking?

Intel's PC Chip Sales Shrink As Server Sales Grow

The contraction is happening in Intel's PC chip business. Segment revenue fell 9% from the prior quarter to $8.1 billion in fiscal Q3 2026. Management expects that figure to fall by more than 20% from there in the fourth quarter, adding that its customers are reducing inventory quickly. Higher memory prices and limited IT budgets are hurting PC sales across the industry, management said, and the company is planning for industry PC unit sales to fall roughly 10% in 2027.

Intel's data center chips are moving the other way. Their revenue was $7.3 billion in the third quarter, up nearly 80% from a year earlier, and management said demand still exceeds supply. Management expects data center revenue to grow quarter over quarter by a mid-teens percentage in the fourth quarter, even though an accident at its Fab 28 factory in Israel will cost about $300 million of revenue in that quarter, almost all of it in server products. So the weaker fourth quarter comes from PCs, while the server business is still expected to grow.

Will Intel Make Cash While It Spends To Grow?

By management's own account, probably not in 2027. On the October 29 call, management called 2027 an investment year, probably without positive free cash flow, as Intel ramps Intel 18A and prepares Intel 14A to begin production in 2028. Gross capital spending is on track for $20 billion in 2026, and management expects it to be up strongly in 2027. Intel ended September with $54.0 billion of cash and short-term investments against $50.1 billion of debt.

The business is more profitable than it was a year ago, but less so than the market as a whole. Over the twelve months to September, Intel kept 10.1% of its sales as operating profit, against 19.0% for the S&P 500. A year earlier, its operating margin was slightly below zero.

Buyers still pay up for Intel's sales: the stock trades at 5.4 times sales, against 3.2 for the S&P 500. A price-to-earnings ratio is not meaningful, because Intel posted a net loss over those twelve months, driven by an $11.0 billion loss in fiscal Q2 2026. In that quarter, Intel still made an operating profit of $1.97 billion, so the loss came from items below operating profit. Buyers paying that price appear to be counting on data center growth lasting through the spending years, and management expects the industry to stay short of supply throughout 2027 and into 2028.
